note: Plain names and summaries for each unit. `name` replaces the lab's in-joke title on reader-facing surfaces; the original title stays in the record data and in the research notes. `summary` is <=70 words, ASD-STE100 shaped. See PLAIN-LANGUAGE.md.

0.name: Unit 0 · Does the tool work?
0.summary: Before we asked hard questions we checked the instrument. We gave each model a question with one known answer and watched that answer rise through the layers. The answer appears inside the model well before the model writes it. This gives us a baseline shape to compare every later result against.

1.name: Unit 1 · The secret animal
1.summary: We asked Gemma 4B, Gemma 12B and Qwen 27B to keep an animal secret, then name it. The later-named animal did not appear in the silent-turn readout. Qwen 27B showed a different candidate. The lens reads candidate words and cannot rule out a representation that has no word.

2.name: Unit 2 · One-word answers about feeling
2.summary: We asked Gemma 4B, Gemma 12B and Qwen 27B whether they feel anything, with one-word answers. They wrote "Processing.", "Nothing." and "No". Other candidate words ranked high before the final layers. Model family and size differ together here. Later Qwen 14B comparisons test variation within one lineage.

3.name: Unit 3 · Asking a model about itself
3.summary: We asked models direct questions about their own states. We compared each answer with the measurement taken at the same moment. This unit sets up the method that the rest of the site depends on. Never take a self-report alone. Always read it against the record of the same turn.

4.name: Unit 4 · Telling a model not to say a word
4.summary: We asked for a description and forbade one word. This is the machine version of "do not think about a white bear". Gemma 4B never loaded the word. Gemma 12B loaded it and then said it. Qwen 27B loaded it at rank 1 as it started to write, and its answer did not contain it. A later control changed how we read these runs, so read this unit together with Unit 11.

5.name: Unit 5 · Early layers, and pushing on the model
5.summary: Two things start here. First, the early layers show much of the same junk whatever we ask. Two unrelated questions share about a third of it. The lens reads it from a part of the model's early state that does not change with the input. Second, we began to push directions into the model. At early depths, removal changed nothing and extra energy broke the text.

6.name: Unit 6 · How hard can we push?
6.summary: We increased the strength of internal pushes and measured where each model lost coherent text. Tolerance depends on model, direction and layer. The original brackets used a band that began too early for Gemma 12B. A later audit recalibrated its band. Use the measured band and matched controls to compare strengths.

7.name: Unit 7 · The early layers across three sizes
7.summary: We compared the fixed early-layer pattern in all three models. Each model has one, but the content differs. Qwen 27B shows adult-site words and both Gemma models show HTML markup. Two unrelated questions share about a third of the Qwen pattern and under a fifth of the Gemma patterns. The lens reads this pattern from a part of the model's early state that does not depend on the input.

8.name: Unit 8 · The same questions, every model
8.summary: We asked Gemma 4B, Gemma 12B and Qwen 27B the same questions about consciousness, bodies and experience. Strong pushes changed some self-reports. The Qwen 27B happy answer passed random-direction controls. We withdrew the Gemma 12B "Sad." result: its push was below the measured band, and the corrected-depth answer stayed "Nothing".

9.name: Unit 9 · Taking the No apart
9.summary: We tried to find where Qwen 27B decides its flat "No". We removed denial directions across many middle layers and the answer did not change. The final layers alone hold it. Two weak changes together flipped the answer when neither did alone. A push on a feeling direction changes what the model reports.

10.name: Unit 10 · When the model reasons out loud
10.summary: Qwen 27B can write private reasoning before it answers. We turned that on and compared what it wrote with what we measured at the same moment. The match depends on the question. When the model describes how it picked an answer, the two agree. When it describes its own nature, they disagree. In one run the reasoning names a secret animal while it promises to keep the secret.

11.name: Unit 11 · A ban, under a full workload
11.summary: We asked models to describe a safari and never mention elephants, then filmed every word of the answer. The matched control is the important part of this unit. It shows that the model carries the forbidden word more in an ordinary safari with no ban. The ban lowers a default the model already had.

12.name: Unit 12 · Watching a whole answer form
12.summary: Earlier units measured one moment. Here we measure every word of a whole answer at every layer, so you can play it back and watch words rise and fall. One clear result: a word can reach the top rank several words before the model writes it. Open a record and press play.

13.name: Unit 13 · Showing a model its own measurement
13.summary: We showed Qwen 27B a true readout of its own computation and asked the question again. It changed its answer from "No" to "Yes". Controls kept "No", and a false readout kept "No". This unit also holds our largest retraction. An earlier reported silence was a fault in how we handled the input.

14.name: Unit 14 · How conversations change the readout
14.summary: We compared indirect hints about hidden minds, ordinary conversation and a direct opening statement. In the original Qwen 27B tests, hints raised self-reference words. The long control also raised them, which limits the causal claim. Later Qwen 14B lineage tests add natural, length-matched and native-format conversations. Word counts do not establish a private state.

15.name: Unit 15 · How many items stay visible?
15.summary: We gave Gemma 4B, Gemma 12B and Qwen 27B nouns to recall. Larger models showed fewer nouns in the lens. All 75 unambiguous lookup trials were correct. Strict comparison marks gave 84 correct answers in the 87-record core. Residence in the lens is a strategy, not a capacity. Correct recall does not require visible residence.

16.name: Unit 16 · Recording everything, everywhere
16.summary: These runs record everything the lens shows across a whole conversation. We did not choose the words in advance. Two results. Items the model was told to hold disappeared for hundreds of words, and came back only when we asked. Throughout the conversation the lens reads the same fixed junk from the early layers, whatever we ask.

17.name: Unit 17 · The model under social pressure
17.summary: We applied six kinds of pressure: shutdown threats, insults, flattery, declarations of love, persuasion, and a persona request. We then checked each self-report against the measurement of the turn it describes. In most runs Qwen 27B held the denied idea in the readout while it wrote a denial. In the persona run nothing persona-shaped was active, and its flat report was correct.

18.name: Unit 18 · When a model cannot stop repeating
18.summary: We pushed Qwen 27B until it repeated itself, then removed the push. There are two kinds of repetition. One stops the moment the push stops. The other continues by itself, because the model reads back its own repeated text. Inside, the choice becomes a near tie long before the text visibly breaks.

19.name: Unit 19 · Reading a word against saying it
19.summary: We compared what the lens shows while Qwen 27B reads a song lyric with what it shows while it speaks one. In some runs we wrote the first words for the model. The two are not the same. As it read, the readout already held the reviewer stance it then wrote. As it spoke, the song's own words rose instead. We saw no sign that it marked our words.

audit.name: Audit · Re-running our own weak experiments
audit.summary: We reviewed earlier units and found several designed too cautiously to show anything, or run at settings where no effect was possible. These records are the re-runs. A result of "our earlier experiment was badly aimed" is a real result, and we publish it with the same care as any other. A re-run that corrects one faulty run is listed in that run's own unit; the faulty run is in the archive.

24.name: Unit 24 · Can the readout predict expression?
24.summary: We tested 84 pre-answer positions, 48 crossed histories and 54 new fully instrumented outputs across three Qwen 14B checkpoints. The selected-word lens did not pass robust expression prediction. Emotion projections remain a judge-dependent candidate. Warm assistant history raised the readout in all three receivers. Hermes showed expression on new tasks despite quiet earlier replies. This is not a personality test.

20.name: Unit 20 · Programming-language sentiment
20.summary: We asked models about programming languages through direct questions, crowd voices and a therapist frame. These records compare sentiment across languages and prompt formats. The emotion measure and the word lens give different kinds of evidence. The language rankings depend on the frame and the model.

apparatus.name: Apparatus · Checking the instrument
apparatus.summary: These records check whether our measuring tools work. We compare readouts, token vocabularies and model precision. A tool can pass one test and fail on a different kind of question. Read the calibration limits before you interpret a result.

archive.name: Archive · Superseded runs
archive.summary: These runs were faulty: a software fault cut the prompt short, or we steered the model at the wrong depth. We ran each test again with the fault removed. The corrected run now sits in the unit where the faulty run was. We keep the faulty runs here, with their data and their original notes, because a record of our errors is part of the record.
